body: This makes sense to me. Any canvas implementers interested? /cc @whatwg/canvas

While it makes sense in the context of this wasm example, I want to note that since reading back memory from the GPU to the CPU is very expensive, an API such as this one would only be a potential improvement if the buffer really needs to be used on the CPU (and not turned back into a graphics object of some sort).
Also, since this operation would be very expensive for GPU canvas implementations, it would make a lot of sense to make it asynchronous. It's not immediately obvious to me how an async version of that would look like, though.

It seems to me that the biggest time spent doing getImageDate is not the copy or creation of the buffer. So it feels like we would be adding a new entry point for performance that doesn't address 90% of the performance problem, which may limit a lot the practical use cases of an api like this.

I came here to file this same issue, as I also think it's an important performance improvement. `WebGLRenderingContext` has `readPixels` which provides a way to fill an existing `ImageData`, but using WebGL for 2D stuff is overkill and not trivial for those (such as myself) unfamiliar with WebGL.

I was going to suggest an existing `ImageData` could be an optional final arg to `getImageData`, but `fillImageData` seems reasonable as well, especially if the API needs to be async.

Perhaps I can provide a more compelling use case. A standard way of getting and using webcam frames is to capture the webcam to a `video` element, then use `drawImage` to draw the frame to a `canvas`, then use `getImageData` to get the `ImageData` object, at which point pixel manipulation can finally be done. If you wanted to add a watermark to video for WebRTC, AFAIK this is the only way to do it. You'd add the watermark then use `putImageData` to put it back to a canvas and then you can use that as the video source.

I have a use-case where I use video from the webcam for barcode scanning using this technique of getting `ImageData` for a webcam frame. It works, but there is a quite a bit of thrashing going on with memory usage due to the fact that trying to keep up with 25 FPS means for a 640x480 video capture you're creating an ~1.2 MB `ImageData` (4 bytes per pixel with RGBA) every frame, totaling 30 MB/sec. This amount of large garbage doesn't play well with the garbage collection. Using the task manager in Chrome I can see that the memory usage for the tab fluctuates quite a bit. This has caused continual problems with lower memory devices, or devices with a high memory usage.

Basically any use-case where you want to use or manipulate webcam data suffers from the performance impact of allocating a new `ImageData` for every frame. [Here is a CodePen](https://codepen.io/anon/pen/QJYJaQ) which simply uses the technique I mentioned above to draw video from a webcam to a canvas, leaving out any actual usage of the `ImageData` (say, for finding and reading a barcode). You can change the variables at the top of the JS to get a finer-grained view of performance. On Chrome 70, I'm seeing memory usage for the tab fluctuating between 115 MB - 190 MB. If you increase the image size to 1280x960, memory usage stays in that same range, but CPU usage for the tab doubles, due to the higher garbage collection workload. If you set the FPS to 1, CPU usage is much lower, and you can watch the memory usage for the tab slowly climb each second until it hits the garbage collection threshold and drops back down. With the proposed `fillImageData`, you'd go from allocating and garbage collecting 30 MB/sec (for 640x480@25 FPS) to a static ~1.2 MB allocation which is reused and requires no garbage collection.

@nical, @fserb, @domenic, any thoughts on this more detailed write-up for a real-world use-case affected by this performance impact? The change would minimize the amount of garbage which otherwise gets created, which is where the performance improvements really come in.
